lesson_title: The GIS in Your Pocket: Layers, Satellites and the Census
hook_text: You ran a full geographic information system last Sunday night — in five seconds, on your phone.
clip_script: Late on a Sunday, someone in your house needs medicine, and you grab a phone and search for a pharmacy that is open. A map slides up: a blue dot for you, pins for the pharmacies, one marked open until ten, and a route threading through the streets toward it. In those five seconds, a complete Geographical Information System ran in your hand. Check it: every pharmacy carries coordinates — georeferenced. Stored on servers. Analysed — filtered for open now, ranked by distance, route computed. Displayed — the map on your screen. And the five components are all there too. Hardware: the phone. Software: the app. Data: every street and opening time — the part that cost fortunes to gather. People: you. Procedures: the update rules that make a new roundabout appear within weeks. One more trick: the app knows WHERE the pharmacy stands — the pin, spatial data — and WHAT it is — name, hours, phone number: attribute data. Tap the pin and the facts unfold. Now scale that up: stack layers of rivers, roads, homesteads and schools over one district, hold the pile to the light, and underserved communities reveal themselves in a glance. That is how planners decide where clinics, standpipes and schools go next.
visual_style: A phone screen glowing in a dark kitchen; the map assembling piece by piece — dot, pins, route; five component labels snapping on; then a zoom-out to translucent map layers stacking over a district with a highlight pulsing on an unserved area.
pacing: Quick relatable open, brisk component checklist, satisfying zoom-out finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for satellites, orthophotos and how the census finds every roof.
